title: The Handoff on St. Mary's Road: How Churton Grove's Fall Actually Starts
summary: A look at how Eno River Farm and Smith's Family Fun Farm split Churton Grove's fall calendar in Hillsborough, NC, plus where residents walk, shop, and eat in between.
body_markdown:
If you've lived in Churton Grove through more than one September, you've probably noticed the same small confusion creep in every year around now: which farm are you supposed to be driving to this weekend? The one with the berries, or the one with the pumpkins? For most of the summer the answer was obvious. Right now it isn't, and that's not a coincidence. It's the point.


Churton Grove's reputation as a neighborhood with real countryside minutes from its gates rests on two farms sitting close together off St. Mary's Road, and the mistake newer residents make is treating them as interchangeable. They're not. Eno River Farm and Smith's Family Fun Farm run on almost opposite calendars, and the switch between them, happening right now, is the closest thing this neighborhood has to a seasonal starting gun.


## Two Farms, Same Road, Different Years


Eno River Farm has been the neighborhood's warm-weather workhorse. Strawberries first, then blueberries, then blackberries, with homemade ice cream running the whole time as the constant. But the farm's own listed activity window doesn't stop when berry season does. It runs from early September through December, and what changes is what's actually in the field. By this point in the year, the same u-pick rows that were roped off for berries in June are more likely to be full of mums. If you've been assuming Eno River Farm is a summer-only stop, you've been skipping the exact stretch where it quietly shifts into a fall destination instead.


Smith's Family Fun Farm runs the inverse pattern, and it runs it hard. This is a farm that has been in the same family for three generations since 1984, built around a pumpkin patch and a cut-your-own Christmas tree operation, and for most of the year it simply isn't the point of anyone's weekend. Its high season is short and specific: pumpkin picking through October, then trees over Black Friday weekend, then quiet again until next fall. That's roughly ten weeks of intensity bracketed by months of dormancy, and if you check its Yelp listing outside that window, as of this past August it was showing up as temporarily closed. That's not neglect. That's just what the farm's calendar looks like when nothing seasonal is happening.


## The Farm That Goes Dark, Then Wakes Up Loud


What makes this year different is that Smith's stopped being purely seasonal. The farm added a Friday night coal-fired pizza series that started earlier in 2026, and it's now renting out the grounds for private events year-round. That's a real change in what the property is for. A farm that used to disappear for eight or nine months at a stretch now has a standing weekly reason to show up even in the off months, which means the handoff between the two farms is starting to blur at the edges even as the core pattern holds.


For residents, that's worth knowing heading into this fall specifically. The pumpkin patch and the tree farm are still the headline events, still packed into that same short window. But if you've written off Smith's as a place you only think about twice a year, the Friday pizza nights are the reason to reconsider that. Check the farm's Facebook page or reach out directly for current dates, since the schedule is still new enough that it isn't locked into a predictable rhythm yet.


## Filling the Space Between Farm Trips


Not every fall weekend needs to end at a farm gate, and Churton Grove has a few reliable ways to fill the gap. Poet's Walk at Ayr Mount is the obvious one: a mile of trail through meadow and woodland next to the historic Ayr Mount home, short enough to fit before dinner and scenic enough that it doesn't feel like a placeholder. It's an easy loop to default to on a weekend when neither farm is calling.


Downtown, the Eno River Farmers Market runs Saturdays year round, with produce, meat, baked goods, and crafts from local growers, and it doubles the value of SNAP benefits spent there, a detail that says something about how the market sees its role in the community beyond just selling vegetables. It's a different kind of farm experience than either Eno River Farm or Smith's, less about picking your own and more about the town showing up in one place once a week.


And when the day ends with dinner instead of a hike, Churton Grove residents tend to split between two answers. Vinny's Italian Grill & Pizzeria covers the comfort-food end, with its ravioli and mozzarella sticks doing most of the reputational work. Hillsborough Bakeshop & Pasta Co, still known to longtime residents by its former name Panciuto, handles the nights that call for something closer to a proper meal, pairing elaborate pasta dishes with baked goods that function as dessert on their own.


## The Clubhouse Goes Quiet Right When the Farms Wake Up


There's a reason the rural side of the neighborhood carries so much weight this time of year, and it has to do with what's happening inside the gates at the same moment. The Churton Grove Clubhouse and pool, the neighborhood's own recreation hub with its tennis and basketball courts, playground, and function room, is built for the warm months. As the pool season winds down, the clubhouse doesn't disappear, but it stops being the default answer to "what are we doing this weekend."


That gap is exactly what the farms are filling right now, and it's also why the conversation around Churton Grove Center has gotten more pointed lately. The Food Lion-anchored strip on Scotswood Boulevard already functions as a landmark for the neighborhood, but residents talking about it on Nextdoor have been fairly direct about wanting more than a grocery run out of it, floating the idea of a coffee shop or a pub as a place to simply get a treat or meet friends. Until that happens, the actual social center of gravity for a Churton Grove weekend still sits outside the neighborhood, on a two-mile stretch of road shared by two farms running opposite clocks.


That's the part worth sitting with as the calendar turns. Churton Grove doesn't have one farm season. It has a relay, and right now is the exact moment the baton is changing hands.
